canberra.title: Is the urban growth boundary pushing up house prices? We’re going to find out
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has agreed to examine whether its proposed urban growth boundary could push up house prices and restrict housing suppl...
canberra.content:
The ACT Government has agreed to assess how its proposed urban growth boundary could affect housing supply and affordability in Canberra. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The ACT Government has agreed to examine whether its proposed urban growth boundary could push up house prices and restrict housing supply, following concerns raised in the Legislative Assembly.

The assessment, due in June 2027, will examine the impact of limiting Canberra’s outward expansion as the government seeks to protect surrounding bushland and environmentally sensitive areas.

The commitment follows a motion from independent MLA Leanne Castley, who warned that restricting new suburban developments without building enough homes in existing suburbs could worsen Canberra’s housing crisis.

Ms Castley said successive governments had failed to deliver enough housing over the past two decades, leaving buyers and renters facing increasingly unaffordable prices.

She told the Assembly that in 1981, a Canberran earning the median income could buy a typical home for around two-and-a-half years of earnings. Today, it would take more than seven years.

She fears an urban growth boundary could further restrict the supply of detached homes and properties with three or more bedrooms, particularly if higher-density development fails to keep up with demand.

“By restricting new greenfields developments in the ACT, an urban growth boundary could mean that we significantly and permanently reduce the supply of new housing,” she said.

“While the intention is to replace greenfields projects with urban infill, I’m not confident that the territory will be able to deliver enough new dwellings to keep up with demand, and I’m not confident that the territory will deliver the types of housing that Canberrans want.”

Ms Castley acknowledged the need to protect environmentally sensitive areas but said the government should examine the costs and benefits before legislating the boundary.

“So with this motion, I’m asking the government to look at the impact of the proposed boundary on supply and affordability before it proceeds to legislation.”

Responding to the motion, Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel confirmed the government would support the assessment.

“Government agrees that there is value in understanding the implications of the urban growth boundary on land supply and housing affordability, considering the impact on the market is an important part of delivering on this policy,” he said.

Mr Steel said work on the boundary was already underway, along with a draft planning and transport strategy and a proposed amendment to the Territory Plan.

The assessment will consider how many more homes could be built in existing suburbs, the availability of land for new suburbs, and the infrastructure needed to support Canberra’s growing population.

Mr Steel said the government wanted more housing close to public transport, jobs and services, including mid-rise apartments, townhouses and other low-rise housing options. He also stressed the importance of protecting Canberra’s hills, ridges, bushland and river corridors.

ACT Greens leader Jo Clay supported the motion but argued that limiting suburban expansion did not necessarily mean higher house prices. She said continued urban sprawl also came at a cost, with new suburbs requiring roads, schools, power lines and water services.

Citing a 2018 government-commissioned study, Ms Clay said the average infrastructure cost of development was approximately $68,000 per home in Whitlam, compared with $6500 in Woden and $23,000 in Campbell.

She argued that Canberra had room for more housing within existing suburbs without sacrificing environmentally significant land.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson also supported the assessment but said housing affordability and environmental protection should not be treated as competing priorities.

Canberra Liberals MLA Deborah Morris also backed the motion, warning that limited land supply was already pushing families towards developments across the NSW border.

She said an independent assessment was needed to understand how the boundary could affect housing costs and the availability of different types of homes.

The assessment is expected to be published alongside the government’s draft planning and transport strategy and proposed urban growth boundary amendment in June 2027, allowing Canberrans to see how the policy could affect housing supply and affordability before the boundary is finalised.

canberra.title: Wildwood is a masterpiece, unfortunately not enough people are seeing it
canberra.snippet: As the film industry grapples with how to use AI and computer-generated imagery becomes more of a crutch, it is rare to find a movie that...
canberra.content:
Wildwood is the latest stop-motion movie from studio Laika. Photo: Laika Entertainment.

As the film industry grapples with how to use AI and computer-generated imagery becomes more of a crutch, it is rare to find a movie that is almost entirely handcrafted.

Thankfully, mercifully, studios like Laika exist and every few years audiences are graced with a new film made using a technique of animation that is tragically dying: stop-motion.

From the brains trust that gave the world movies like Coraline and Kubo and the Two Strings, Laika’s new film Wildwood has finally hit cinemas after 14 years in development.

The almost entirely stop-motion film follows Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee), a teenage girl who lives a fairly sheltered life thanks to her superstitious parents.

Reluctantly, Prue is tasked with babysitting her baby brother, Mac, with the condition that they must stay at home.

In typical teenage fashion, Prue ignores this direction and instead rides her bike into the city with her brother trailing on the back.

The siblings run into Prue’s classmate Curtis (Jacob Tremblay), who tags along on their adventure. During a stop at the playground, Mac is picked up and carried away by a magical murder of crows that take him into the mysterious forest on the outskirts of town.

After passing the fog, Prue and Curtis enter a mythical new world called Wildwood, which is filled with talking animals, strange tribes and warring factions.

It’s here they learn of the former Dowager Governess of Wildwood, Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), who has turned to using dark magic and threatens to destroy Wildwood.

Now, that is a lot of synopsis to give away, but it’s all information learnt in the first 15-20 minutes of the film and it’s all important to understand just how grand this movie is.

Clearly taking inspiration from Narnia and Lord of the Rings, Wildwood is epic in every sense of the word.

The world it creates is fantastic. The characters range from wacky to wonderful and the scope of adventure is truly awe-inspiring.

All of these points are only amplified by the complete artistry of the film’s model work and stop-motion technique.

I have seen more than 2500 movies in my life and even still, I can’t begin to understand how this thing was made.

Upon researching, over 1000 artists worked on the film. More than 142,000 face models were created, over 200 puppets were designed and over 1150 days were spent filming each individual frame.

It is a true marvel of animated filmmaking and is unlike anything ever made before it from a production standpoint.

In addition to the incredible animation, the movie has a fantastic score orchestrated by Dario Marianelli. It never lets up throughout the two hour plus runtime.

For my fellow gamers out there, it took me back to the newer God of War games with its almost Nordic sound and sweeping use of strings and horns.

The voice acting is also top-notch. Lee and Tremblay prove why they are actors to watch for the future and Mulligan turns in a performance akin to the White Witch from The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

While the production side of things might be perfect, there are some slight issues with the film’s structure.

The middle act has some pacing issues, relating mainly to how information is delivered and how characters move from point A to point B.

It’s very minor, especially in a film as grand as this, but it’s worth pointing out. When a movie is as methodical as Wildwood is during its first half, it gives a bit of a whiplash effect when people are forced around quickly.

It’s rectified by the film’s final act, with the last 30 minutes being the best sequence I’ve seen in a movie this year.

There are also issues with the characterisation of Prue’s parents. There is a reveal at the start of the final act that contextualises a lot of what is going on, but the way Prue’s parents react to this information felt unreasonable given how they were presented prior to this moment.

With that said, these issues almost mean nothing when the film shoots back into full gear. It’s emotional, inspiring and probably the most visually stunning thing you’ll see on a movie screen this decade.

Wildwood is a true masterpiece of artistic filmmaking and unless you’re actively looking for critiques, you won’t find any.

I pray people will go out and see this film to keep the art of stop-motion alive, but if it’s opening weekend box office haul of $11 million on a $100 million budget is anything to go by, it sadly doesn’t look great.

Wildwood is showing in cinemas across the country. Please go and see it on the biggest screen you can!

canberra.title: From traffic jams to gang-gang cockatoos: Why Telopea Park School’s expansion has locals concerned
canberra.snippet: Five hundred more students, an 81-space carpark and a new double gymnasium. Canberra’s biggest public high school is preparing to g...
canberra.content:
The proposed $53.4 million Telopea Park School expansion has raised concerns among local residents over traffic, parking and green space. Photo: Facebook.

Five hundred more students, an 81-space carpark and a new double gymnasium. Canberra’s biggest public high school is preparing to grow, but its neighbours are asking a different question: What will happen to the streets, playing fields and green spaces around it?

The proposed $53.4 million expansion of Telopea Park School has drawn concerns from inner-south residents, with a newly released community consultation report revealing worries about traffic congestion, parking shortages, loss of recreational space and the impact on nearby homes.

While many residents support better facilities for students, they are questioning whether the surrounding neighbourhood can accommodate a much larger school without compromising road safety and residential amenity.

Traffic and parking emerged as the most frequently raised issues during consultation. Residents described existing congestion during school drop-off and pick-up times and warned that additional students could worsen conditions in New South Wales Crescent, Fitzroy Street and surrounding roads.

The proposed 81-space carpark has divided opinion. Some believe additional parking is essential, while others question whether it will be sufficient or whether the project should instead encourage greater use of public transport, cycling and walking.

Suggestions included dedicated drop-off zones, safer pedestrian crossings and changes to traffic circulation.

Residents also want to know how construction vehicles will navigate the area, where workers will park and how disruption to surrounding homes and school operations will be managed.

But the debate goes beyond traffic. The expansion will occupy neighbouring land currently used as a playing field, raising concerns about the future of one of the area’s recreational spaces. The land is used not only by students but also by residents, dog walkers and other community members.

Some participants questioned whether enough outdoor space would remain for children to play and exercise once the new facilities were built. Others called for more trees, additional shade and landscaping to compensate for the changes.

The environmental concerns extended to mature trees and wildlife habitat, with several submissions specifically mentioning gang-gang cockatoos. Residents want to know how the project will protect biodiversity and whether existing trees can be retained.

Locals also called for stronger sustainability measures, including solar panels, renewable energy, all-electric buildings, electric vehicle charging stations and water-sensitive urban design. They encouraged the government to increase tree canopy and landscaping, making environmental performance a central consideration in the final design.

The expansion follows a significant decision about the future of public education in Canberra’s inner south. In 2023, the ACT Government decided against building a new high school in the area, opting instead to expand Telopea Park School to accommodate an additional 500 students.

It is already the Territory’s largest public high school, with 1056 students in Years 7 to 10, according to the 2026 school census.

Across all year levels, it has 1595 students enrolled, against an existing capacity of 1784.

Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel has approved rezoning neighbouring land from restricted-access recreation to community facility use, allowing the expansion to proceed through the planning process.

The proposed development includes specialist classrooms, a multipurpose hall incorporating a double gymnasium, additional parking and improved connections between the existing school and new facilities.

However, the size and location of the buildings have raised another set of concerns among residents living closest to the site. Apartment owners and tenants questioned how the new structures would affect privacy, views and natural light, while others raised the possibility of noise from the gymnasium and after-hours activities.

They sought details about building heights, separation distances, fencing and acoustic treatments. A small number also expressed concerns about potential impacts on property values.

The school’s heritage setting has added another dimension to the debate. While some participants welcomed the proposed design, others argued that such a prominent location deserved architecture that better reflected the character of the existing school and surrounding neighbourhood.

There was also considerable support for allowing the wider community to use the new sporting facilities.

However, residents want clearer answers about operating hours, bookings, security and whether evening and weekend activities would create additional parking and noise problems.

The consultation recorded 249 face-to-face interactions across seven engagement sessions, alongside online comments and written submissions. The sessions covered both the school expansion and the proposed Inner South Health Centre.

Despite the concerns, the report found broad support for the project’s educational benefits and the prospect of additional sporting and community facilities.

The ACT Government says feedback will inform further design work, alongside traffic assessments, environmental studies and other technical investigations. A development application is yet to be lodged, giving residents another opportunity to examine the detailed plans and make submissions.

canberra.title: How about this weather? Rain, hail or shine, it’s all hard work
canberra.snippet: Right now, backyards, nature strips and paddocks around Canberra are looking as green and picturesque as a scene from Sound of Music. It’...
canberra.content:
It’s a pleasure to see our bush capital looking so lush, though taming the wild greenery is no walk in the park. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Right now, backyards, nature strips and paddocks around Canberra are looking as green and picturesque as a scene from Sound of Music.

It’s hard to believe just a few short years ago it was more like Mad Max.

But far from singing and dancing atop a mountain, I’m sweating it out on the mower, fighting a losing battle against weeds and repairing our weathered trampoline following its recent unapproved travel into the neighbour’s yard.

This climate of extremes is a full-time gig.

In fairness, twirling around wildly with eyes skyward is inadvisable on an Aussie mountaintop. If I saw someone doing this atop Booroomba Rocks, I simply would not sing an endearing song about them. I would give them a stern safety briefing and a lifetime bushwalking ban.

Over recent weeks, large parts of eastern Australia have been put on alert for severe thunderstorms, with warnings issued from the Queensland border down to the Snowy Mountains.

Of course, some of those storms turned out to be moths. But many were definitely notable weather events, from Ulladulla’s tiny (yet damaging) tornado to Canberra’s tree-toppling Sunday storms.

In general, Australia generally has famously good weather, until we don’t. And we don’t do things by halves. I swear everyday there’s a news report claiming it’s been the hottest, wettest, driest, rainiest season on record.

Speaking of which, the ACT this year experienced the warmest winter on record.

Our "dam", February 2020. Photos: Hayley Nicholls

Now burgeoning with life (and snakes), November 2027.

Urging residents to do the work of preparing for the projected storm season, ACTSES Chief Officer Steve Forbes said: “Dry days and warm temperatures often create atmospheric conditions that intensify storms with no notice, and they can do really big damage to you, your family and your property.”

Ah, ‘Straya. We might enjoy carefree days of cracking barbecue weather, but the roof might blow off our house that night.

And if it’s not the barometer giving us trouble, it’s the seasonal extremes of our wildlife.

I think I’ve made my stance on moths quite clear.

The heat also brings out our impressive array of cold-blooded creatures. For example, the eight species of snakes which call the ACT home. Of these, five are venomous and considered dangerous to humans. Bit extreme, innit?

But snakes are not our only enemy hidden in plain sight. And no, I’m not talking politics. We also have an extremely high pollen count (just when you thought we couldn’t get any nerdier).

In drought conditions, we’re setting timers to give our gardens a medicinal drop of water. Or getting bushfire ready by clearing, pruning, and mowing – sometimes at the crack of dawn or late at night to limit the possibility of a singular spark with deadly consequences.

Too many of us still remember the frantic work of blocking gutters and filling bathtubs in January 2003.

On the flip side, too much rain sees our landscape flooded with red-capped mushrooms, which look magical, but are – you guessed it – poisonous.

On occasion I still spot a vintage Canberra car which has clearly never recovered from the great hailstorm of 2020, when insurance companies nationwide cursed the capital as hailstones the size of public servants pelted our plentiful outdoor carparks.

Suddenly, our pollen problems are looking even lamer.

Of course, we can make the best of things whatever the weather. Thunderstorms are a cosy backdrop for curling up with Netflix or a book, grey days are great for gardening, and sunshine makes for a cracking party. Wind sucks – I have nothing good to say about wind (Pollen’s partner-in-crime).

But whatever the weather in this land of extremes, nobody has time to truly enjoy it. There’s too much to prepare for, or recover from.

It may look lusher than a Swiss mountaintop out there, but nobody’s frolicking.

Because the hills are alive, but that’s not music. It’s snakes. Time to get on the mower again.

canberra.title: Stop and smell the history at Old Parliament House’s rose gardens
canberra.snippet: Flower enthusiasts can learn about horticulture and history as the National and Old Parliament House rose gardens show off their vibrant ...
canberra.content:
The Old Parliament House rose gardens are in full bloom, with tours available for bookings throughout November. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Flower enthusiasts can learn about horticulture and history as the National and Old Parliament House rose gardens show off their vibrant and fragrant beauty throughout November.

The National Rose Gardens received an upgrade in 2025 and were recently formally re-opened to the public.

Visitors will notice new rose varieties scattered among the beds, which represent each state and territory of Australia.

National Capital Authority Horticultural Projects senior officer Brad Doherty explained this was able to happen as the previous flowers weren’t heritage-listed.

“Only the colour and layout of the garden beds are heritage-listed so then, when you look at that from an aerial shot, it looks like a rose petal opening,” he said.

“That’s why those garden beds are in a round circle motion out there.”

Hybrid tea roses are the main breeds chosen for the National Rose Gardens as part of the refresh.

Mr Doherty said they tried to choose varieties that were more suitable for Canberra’s climate.

“[We also considered] climate change in that equation, as we’re going to get hotter summers, warmer winters and all that kind of stuff, so we’ve picked roses that will tolerate that out there a lot more,” he said.

“My favourite one [in those gardens] is Golden Child … it’s a bright yellow rose, it’s quite spectacular.”

If you’re after more information about roses, step across the road from the National Rose Gardens and step into the ones around Old Parliament House.

There are more than 4000 bushes in bloom throughout November, from across 500 varieties.

They pay homage to famous people including Queen Elizabeth II, William Shakespeare, Sir Donald Bradman, Princess of Wales, Dame Elisabeth Murdoch, Fred Hollows, Jayne Austin, Mary Queen of Scots, Leonardo de Vinci and Elizabeth Arden, among others.

Mr Doherty said the Abraham Lincoln was his favourite rose within the garden walls.

“It’s got a good balance of smell, the colour, and it’s very big,” he explained.

“[The flower itself] sort of goes from a darker red on the outer edge as it ages, and then the smell’s quite outstanding on it too.

“So it’s a good, round, balanced rose – where some of the new roses you have, they lose their colour. They have brighter colour [but] lose their scent.”

Some of the rare varieties include the Butterfly Rose or Rosa chinensis ‘Mutabilis’, a hardy rose from China famous for flowers that continuously change colour from yellow-apricot to pink and deep crimson.

Mr Doherty said it had never been hybridised or bred with other varieties, making it very unique.

“The colour changes are exactly like what it does in the wild, so when it was found in the wild and before it came into cultivation and spread across the world, it would have done that exact same thing,” he said.

The Persian-Damask rose (Rosa Damascena) is the most fragrant rose in the world, whose scent has been captured and preserved in the form of rose oil and rose water dating back to ancient times in the Middle East.

For those wanting to learn more about the history of the rose varieties – and the gardens themselves – tours are being held every Tuesday and Sunday throughout November.

Mr Doherty said there was always something different to learn about the garden’s 99-year history.

“There’s a lot of major history through the gardens, but also [about] the collection of the roses we have,” he said.

All the perfect excuse to stop and smell the roses.

Old Parliament House rose garden tours are held at 9:30 am each Tuesday and Sunday in November. Tickets can be purchased here.

australia.title: I spent the first day of the south-west metro’s life exploring the delights of the line. Now I want to move closer
australia.snippet: My relationship with Sydney’s delayed metro extension is complicated. But on Friday, as I caught a regular bus home, I daydreamed of movi...
australia.content:
I’ve already been awake for six hours when I jump off the metro back at Bankstown station at 8.33am on Friday. It’s the first day of driverless trains running on the extension from Bankstown to Sydenham and I was on the first service heading into the city at 4.31am.

The trip on the new track took just 21 minutes in the wee hours. Now I’m exploring the line at a more leisurely pace. I’m not sure what meal I should be eating as I stumble into An Restaurant before 9am. It’s widely considered to serve some of Sydney’s best pho.

In Vietnam, the noodle soup is typically eaten for breakfast, and the dirty dishes trolley is already stacked with bowls scraped clean by customers. The restaurant is buzzing with metro staff celebrating the culmination of two years’ hard work.

Sleep-deprived and feeling adventurous, I order the option with beef tendon ($21) which arrives in minutes.

Tendon, I conclude, is not for me, but the broth is rich and restorative, as is the iced coffee with condensed milk ($8). There’s a pep in my step as I stroll back up Bankstown City Plaza. Boxes of fish are off-loaded from trucks, vendors sell herbs from the pavement and people chat in cafes.

Unlike the city metro’s architectural marvels, Bankstown is the only new station on the south-west line. The pale-brick rectangular structure is functional, but hides a secret. Behind one facade are heritage buildings from the original station which now hosts trains running west on the T6 heavy rail line.

Outside the station, half a dozen pink replacement buses sit quietly. They are still operating on Friday and the opening weekend, while communities adjust, but they’re mostly empty.

My relationship with Sydney’s south-west metro extension is complicated. Over two years, I and everyone else waited for a line that was only meant to take 12 months to complete.

I moved from Dulwich Hill not long after the previous heavy rail line closed in September 2024 but moved back last year to Marrickville, one stop down the line.

After 12 months of queuing for those pink buses, I moved away again this year, thinking there was no end in sight to the conversion project.

Instant relief

Friday’s opening provided instant relief for commuters travelling to and from the south-western suburbs.

The driverless trains already in use from Tallawong through the city to Sydenham have been cleaned and updated with signage to reflect the 10 new stops to Bankstown. On a clear, bright morning, the wide windows at each end offer an unencumbered view of the suburbs.

Arriving at Lakemba, three stops and six minutes from Bankstown, I find a single man queuing for the pink buses. I ask why.

“I don’t know why. Is the train open?” he asks hopefully. He abandons the bus stop and heads up the station stairs.

I walk along Haldon Street, which hosts the Lakemba Nights market during Ramadan, with vendors stretching north towards the Lakemba mosque.

On Friday, I head south, paying $14 for a selection of baklava and pastries from Lebanese desert shop King of Sweets. One, deep fried and filled with custard, sends me into a sugary reverie. I sit, listening to people converse in Arabic, before heading into the station.

Campsie at 10.38am

Two stops and four minutes later, I’m at Beamish Street in Campsie. Sadly, I’m already stuffed, so can’t contemplate the Chinese, Indian, Japanese, Korean and Malaysian street food on offer. My stomach and I will be back.

Instead, I search for some fresh fruit. There’s a market on Sundays but now I head to a greengrocer on Anzac Mall. I land on a Chinese Fuji, a Ya pear, a custard apple and an Indian bittermelon (yes, the latter being a vegetable).

Mid-morning on a Friday, Campsie is heaving. A couple of weeks ago, the metro station at the centre of the suburb was behind wire fencing and the only still point.

Three stops from Campsie, and another six minutes down the line, and I’m back on the platform at Dulwich Hill, where I last caught a train more than two years ago.

Like the other stations on the line, the heritage buildings have been retained, with lifts added for accessibility.

The most visible difference is the addition of glass barriers along the edge of the platform which are universal along the metro line.

One of the challenges of converting the 130-year-old south-west extension has been the need to add mechanical “gap-fillers” to, well, fill the space between the metro trains and the exisiting curved platforms. Particularly wide gaps at three doors at Dulwich Hill mean they will remain closed while data is collected on the reliability of the gap-fillers.

Something else that’s changed since I left is the completion of the GreenWay, a 6km pedestrian and cycling corridor from Iron Cove to the Cooks River, which the state government likes to claim “intersects” with the metro.

This is kind of true. In reality, the GreenWay passes near Dulwich Hill’s metro station, rather than connecting to it. After squeezing past a construction truck down a road in need of resurfacing, I find the cycleway, but there’s a lack of signage.

I’m on a Lime bike, which I’ve never ridden before. I’ve been somewhat suspicious of the shared ebike scheme and I’m not encouraged after the app tells me the bike I choose is unavailable, despite it being right there in front of me.

I reluctantly settle for one with McDonald’s wrappers and old chewing gum stuck to the basket.

But, once I’m riding on the GreenWay, with the wind in my hair and the sun on my face, I’m converted. I start to imagine I am the Sydney metro: driverless and travelling at speed through the inner west, my cares slip away.

Marrickville at 12.02pm

When I step back onto the metro at Dulwich Hill and turn to face the doors, I feel a hand on my shoulder. A man further down has tried to leave through one of the doors that won’t open at this platform and now I’m in his way as he hurries for an exit.

Given the metro travels at up to 100km/h, we’re at Marrickville in less than two minutes. This part of the sprawling suburb, along Illawarra and Marrickville roads, is known less for its breweries than its bars, late-night venues and restaurants.

People queue for banh mi at Marrickville Pork Roll or rice paper rolls at Banh Cuon Ba Oanh, while enormous joints of roast lamb and pork sit steaming in trays at the Corinthian Rotisserie Restaurant.

I step, instead, into the secondhand clothes shop Uturn, one of several vintage and op shops along the strip. Uturn has another location at Punchbowl, one stop from Bankstown, where you can buy clothes by the kilo for $10.

I browse through niche football shirts and spy a T-shirt with a rude pun. I don’t buy anything: I’ve spent all my money on fruit, pastries and tendon.

As I doze on a regular, rather than pink, bus home, I dream about moving again. To be close to the metro.

australia.title: Home values fall for seventh consecutive month as interest rates dent demand
australia.snippet: Centre of downturn shifts away from Sydney and Melbourne, but after such strong growth most homeowners still sit on sizeable gains Get ou...
australia.content:
Australian home values have dropped for a seventh consecutive month, with prices in the capital cities now falling at the fastest pace in 40 years as rising mortgage rates scare off buyers.

Cotality data shows the centre of the downturn is also shifting away from Sydney and Melbourne toward the mid-sized state capital cities, with Brisbane and Perth leading October’s declines.

Combined values across the state and territory capital cities fell 1.4% over the month.

Cotality’s research director, Tim Lawless, said the downturn was now broad-based, with capital city home values down 8.1% since March.

“The mid-sized capitals, where home values recorded extreme growth conditions over the past six years, are now well and truly in a correction,” Lawless said.

“Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in value over the past three months.”

The property market has been weighed down by four interest rate hikes this year, with a fifth widely expected when the Reserve Bank hands down its decision on Tuesday.

Most economists anticipate double-digit falls in Australian property prices as interest rates climb, with Morgan Stanley forecasting peak-to-trough drops of up to 15%.

Lawless said high interest rates were the “most significant downside influence”, while affordability challenges and a pullback in investors sparked by the government’s tax changes had also dented demand.

Although the pace of decline is at four-decade highs, Lawless said that largely reflected how strong the property market had been over the period.

Australian home prices started to decouple from wages in the late 1980s, before a surge in the 90s and early 2000s propelled the country into a state of unaffordable housing exacerbated by investor-friendly tax settings that were only recently unwound.

Over the past decade, property prices have doubled – or nearly doubled – in Adelaide, Brisbane, Perth and Hobart. They are up by more than 50% in Canberra, and more than 30% in Sydney and Darwin. Prices are up by just over 20% in Melbourne.

Most homeowners are still sitting on sizeable gains despite the recent weakness. Even a 20% drop in Perth prices from their record high would only take the market back to mid-2025 levels, according to Cotality analysis.

Peter Esho, an economist and chief executive at 13x, said he believed the big housing markets of Sydney and Melbourne were “close to bottoming”, while the mid-sized capitals were at an earlier stage of the downturn.

“The downturn is just part of a normal housing cycle, driven by interest rates, which are having a negative wealth effect,” Esho said.

“They’re really denting sentiment, and real estate is a sentiment asset.”

Esho said he did not believe the price falls would turn “systemic”, which he said would only happen if it became difficult for prospective buyers to borrow, like it did in the US during the global financial crisis, or if unemployment surged.

Rental pressures have eased slightly, with national vacancy rates rising and rent growth slowing, according to Cotality.

Rents are still up more than 50% over six years, adding about $245 a week to the median rental rate, fast outpacing wage growth.

Analysts partly link the rising vacancy rate to changing household dynamics. Driven by affordability, more renters are sharing homes or moving in with family, unwinding the pandemic-driven shift toward smaller households with room for a home office.

australia.title: Former NSW Liberal leads overhaul of One Nation candidate selection process
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Mark Jones, once on track for one of the Liberal party’s most powerful roles, is now instrumental in One Nation’s expansion Ge...
australia.content:
In 2023, a young and ambitious Liberal moderate was on the brink of securing one of the most powerful roles in the party: state director of the New South Wales branch. Three years later, he is playing a key role in selecting and vetting One Nation candidates determined to beat his former colleagues.

Multiple Liberal sources familiar with recruitment for the position, which involves running election campaigns and managing fundraising, confirm Mark Jones was among the final three candidates for the role before his career advancement was ultimately blocked.

Internal One Nation documents seen by Guardian Australia show Jones – who quit the Liberal party in January – has become integral to One Nation’s state election campaigns performing similar administrative functions.

Since joining One Nation as a political consultant in February, Jones has helped redesign the party’s candidate selection and vetting process and sat in on interviews. He is being assisted by former Queensland National party executive Susie Douglas, who briefly worked for the Palmer United Party before quitting and describing it as a cult.

The changes have not stopped One Nation endorsing several state candidates with controversial backgrounds, however. These include a former Liberal who has won support from alleged underworld figures, a naturopath who has endorsed Donald Trump’s unfounded claim that paracetamol is linked to autism and a former shire councillor who lost his licence for drink-driving.

On Sunday, the One Nation candidate for Melbourne, Matthew Collins, resigned and apologised for now deleted comments on social media regarding a number of issues including sexual consent and pornographic jokes. A party spokesperson said the comments were “offensive”.

Guardian Australia can reveal One Nation has also overhauled its candidate selection process in NSW after being criticised by some members in Victoria for lengthy delays and a lack of democratic decision making.

Victorian applicants who were invited to short online interviews with Jones and Douglas were surprised to find the state party leader, Warren Pickering, was also in attendance. Internal documents show the three-person team was a “selection committee”. Endorsement decisions were made after police and credit checks.

In NSW, 20-30 minute interviews are now being conducted by Jones and Douglas alone, who then make recommendations to a three-person selection committee that does not include them. The committee members are the NSW leader, Mike Newman, the state president, Rebecca Thompson, and the state secretary, Sam Donovan.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

These online interviews test candidate ideas for the future of the state, their knowledge of the parliamentary system and how they could contribute to a future One Nation government.

“You are expected to address each of these matters,” states a document seen by Guardian Australia. “Please treat this invitation and your participation in the selection process as confidential. Please do not announce or publish your participation at this stage.”

In Victoria, applicants were first screened with a 25-page form that included detailed questions including whether someone had been subject to court proceedings or accused of bullying and verbal abuse. In NSW, this has been streamlined to a much shorter online questionnaire.

The NSW branch has also introduced a requirement for candidates to include a 60-second video of themselves outlining why they want to join the party, after finding Victorian candidates who looked good on paper but were not up to scratch when interviewed.

These changes may not be enough to satisfy some One Nation members who would like branches to have a greater say in who is selected to represent their regions.

In September, Newman said One Nation had already received 900 applications for 93 NSW seats. Earlier this month, the party called for more applications before the 31 October deadline.

Before interviews are conducted, applicants must sign restrictive non-disclosure agreements that are not imposed by any other parties. This stops them from publicly confirming their applications.

A copy of a non-disclosure agreement used in NSW confirms candidates may be held financially liable should they share or fail to appropriately secure confidential party information.

From moderate Liberal to One Nation whisperer

Guardian Australia has spoken to several NSW Liberal sources who described Jones as a professional operator who retains close ties to the party.

Some expressed frustration he no longer worked for the Liberals and disappointment that a moderate would help One Nation’s campaigns against his former colleagues.

Jones is a former deputy chief of staff to the NSW Liberal minister Don Harwin, who was a leading moderate at the time. He was also an unsuccessful Liberal candidate for the state seat of Shellharbour in 2015.

After leaving state parliament in 2019, Jones joined the lobbying firm PremierNational and worked alongside another moderate powerbroker, Michael Photios.

In early 2026, Jones formed his own political consultancy firm with his wife, Shani, who also previously worked for a NSW Liberal minister and has since been contracted to One Nation.

South Australian electoral records show that firm, Camelot Consulting, was paid more than $100,000 for services to One Nation during the state election in March. It is not yet known how much money Camelot has earned from the party in NSW and Victoria.

Documents seen by Guardian Australia show Douglas is working as “candidate selection officer”. She describes herself as a “former senior vice president of the National party in Queensland”.

After serving as an independent councillor on the Gold Coast, Douglas unsuccessfully contested the federal seat of McPherson in Queensland for the Palmer United party in 2013.

A year later, she told the Gold Coast Bulletin that Clive Palmer’s party was “a bit like being in a cult – everyone in his group looks up to him”.

One Nation, Jones and Douglas declined to comment.

australia.title: Odette on a later-in-life autism diagnosis: ‘It completely revolutionised the way that I exist’
australia.snippet: Last year, she got sober and an official diagnosis. It’s not the first time a new understanding about herself has reframed the Sydney art...
australia.content:
In 2021, just before the release of her second album, Sydney singer-songwriter Odette – full name Georgia Odette Sallybanks – was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. As she said at the time, this threw new light on the songs she had written in the murky depths of constant rumination. She renamed the album from Dwell to Herald – reframing from slippery interiority to public declaration – and threw herself into the promo cycle with more ruthless honesty than ever.

That rawness, and her signature dance between rich vocal runs and loping spoken-word rhythms, has won her fans worldwide, as well as four Aria nominations. Her first two records, including 2018 debut To A Stranger, were released on the major label that signed her when she was still a teenager, and one of the most hyped young songwriters in the country.

The five years between Herald and her upcoming third LP, Blink, would be informed by another diagnosis shattered and rebuilt the picture again.

“Reframing has been the whole purpose of this record,” she says. “And Jesus Christ, my brain is different.”

We’re sitting on a bench in a harbourside park in Sydney, not far from her shared flat. The water is sparkling, the sky is blue; a magpie trots past with a primo shred of golden croissant in its beak, and a delighted Sallybanks stops mid-sentence to congratulate it. She is animated and Zen as our conversation loops between the sunny topics (her girlfriend, the piano, crafting her own stage set out of cardboard at home) and the grimmer ones (genocides, billionaires, Ed Sheeran).

“I’m both relaxed and careful at the same time,” she says. “It’s such a good feeling, in my body: not drinking, just focusing on music and my relationships, and going outside, and I feel like a goddam newborn baby … Colours are brighter!”

In 2024, Sallybanks parted ways with her label and began writing and recording with her friend, songwriter-producer Kiah Gossner.

“I was very mentally ill – I think I was still going in and out of psychosis when we started the album, but the record itself wasn’t necessarily marinating in it. It was lifting me out of it,” she says, describing her creative partnership with Gossner as “one of the most freeing experiences of my life”.

In July that year she released the single Reverence on tiny indie label Beloved Records, and kept writing with Gossner. Then in mid-2025, within a short space of time, Sallybanks got two things: sober, and an official autism diagnosis.

Sallybanks was fine with the news; it was her mother who cried when she heard. On top of historical gaps in awareness of how autism presents in girls, doctors had also been blaming her behavioural issues on racist assumptions about her mother, who is a South African woman with Zulu heritage, she says. “My whole life, she was just trying to get me help, and there was none, and look what happened,” Sallybanks says. “I tried to numb myself in substance abuse – I think that was my way of [masking] – and I ended up in all the wrong places, and it destroyed my body and it destroyed my mind.”

Early intervention is “so crucial to the success of autistic people,” she says – and a later-in-life diagnosis can feel a bit like being handed an Xbox controller after decades of trying to play with a battered TV remote. Sallybanks says that while she can’t change past behaviour she’s ashamed of, or get back the time that feels lost, she now feels like she’s finally “shown up to [her] own life”.

“It completely revolutionised the way that I exist,” she says. “It’s revolutionised my music, my business skills, my friendships, my relationships, everything.”

Musicians who depart a well-resourced major label will often wax ambivalent about the joys and pressures of handling more things on your own. Sallybanks is the first artist I’ve ever heard use the word “mycelial” to describe the process. “It’s like the roots of [an album cycle] extend beyond the creative – organising tours and doing everything that usually I would have had a lot more support with,” she says. This theme runs through the record like a root system: progress through necessary rot, growth that has gnarliness and ugliness to it rather than pink-bud innocence.

Desiccated, wild textures thread through the lyrics – “Alencon lace / all dried remains”; “was I just a briar that your sleeve was snagged on?” – interspersed with contrasting squishes of mud and primordial goo. The album cover, by artist Oscar Davis, is a pyrographic sketch of impossible delicacy on a cardboard panel, ripped corrugated edges visible. There’s something pleasingly perverse about drawing a plant using fire on the remains of other, deader plants, another strange loop, beauty through breakdown. “I used to think there was so much value in whether people were thinking I was beautiful, and whether people thought I was like, sexy and cool,” she says. “And now I feel like I’ve really embraced just being feral.”

Her molasses-rich voice has never been better framed – the spareness of her first two records has relaxed and let life get in through the cracks, with oboes hunting around the edges and syncopated jumbles that had me hunting down old Tuneyards albums for a revisit. (Associated Bandcamp tags and Spotify mix tapes reference “gutter folk” and “trash pop”.)

Her other tic as a composer-arranger are – back around again – circles and loops. On a line by line level she favours these claw-handed little ostinatos, spiky and teasing (like the one that hooks you in from the beginning of her 2017 debut single Watch Me Read You) and I ask if she’s conscious of the habit, or has a name for it. She does, actually. It’s Eric.

“He just comes out and shreds, and then he’s like, ‘All right, bye!’” she laughs. “I wrote a lot of this piano when I was, like, super duper manic. So playing it back and learning it now, in my normal life, is like ‘Why? Why did I do this?” (“Take it away, Eric!” she cries on standout track Seahorses, before, well, shredding.)

Blink also starts and ends on the same note – in a nod to one of her biggest influences, Joanna Newsom, who does the same on Divers – “to pay homage to this idea that we are constantly circling the same idea.”

An idea that Sallybanks keeps circling: that just as she can be both relaxed and careful nobody is ever just one thing. “I’m a woman, and I’m brown, and I’m autistic, and I’m all these things. But I’m talking about being alive. Everybody knows what that feels like,” she says.

“Even the quietest person, we do violence against ourselves – we abuse substances, we yell at each other when we’ve got road rage.” Community and creativity, she insists, can rebuild some of what we’ve lost.

“There’s all this anger festering inside us, and we have all these little outlets [we could use to channel it]… I think that that’s what I’m trying to sing to. We’re all kind. We’re all terrible and kind, and we get to – we decide for ourselves how we want to live.”

Blink by Odette is out 6 November via Beloved Records

Odette’s songs to live by

What music do you clean the house to?

At the moment I do most things to Choke Enough by Oklou. It helps me relax.

What’s the song you wish you wrote?

I don’t really think like that. I really love the song Nausicaa’ by Cameron Winter.

If your life was a movie, what would the opening credits song be?

Ghosts by Japan or Cores by Da Lata – maybe that’s the end credits though.

What’s a song you can never listen to again?

I especially listen to those ones because I argue with my own limitations every day. It’s hard to listen to Cosmia by Joanna Newsom even though it’s one of my favourite songs.

What classic song should be stripped of its title?

I Just Called To Say I Love You. That song is like being stuck in a lift.

What is the first song/album you bought?

The first proper album I ever bought myself I think was Cherry Depression by Beach House. But if we’re going way back to iTunes, probably something by Justin Bieber.

What song do you want played at your funeral?

Excellent question. I want my corpse to do an animatronic strip tease to Angel Of The Morning by Juice Newtown.

What is the best song to have sex to?

Frühlingstimmen by Johann Strauss.

australia.title: Northern Territory water plan condemned as ‘blatant and shameless’ attack on nature
australia.snippet: Exclusive : Move to scrap legal requirement to set aside water for environment is ‘extreme even for the NT CLP government’, green group s...
australia.content:
The Northern Territory government has been accused of making a “blatant and shameless” attack on nature by planning to delete a legal requirement that water must be allocated to the environment.

In what has been described as the latest in a series of attacks on the environment by the NT’s Country Liberal party, the Finocchiaro government plans to change water rules that govern how much ground and surface water industry can take.

It comes as the government plans a major expansion of fracking, datacentres and agricultural development.

The Wilderness Society chief executive, Kirsty Howey, said the latest move was “extreme even for the NT CLP government”. She called on the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, to withhold commonwealth water funding if the bill passed.

The Central Land Council, which represents Indigenous people in the southern half of the NT, said the territory government was trying to “covertly” remove the last remaining protections Territorians had in the use and management of water.

The council’s chief executive, Les Turner, said: “It is actively undermining community aspirations for improved and transparent water planning laws. This flies in the face of national trends and ignores the voices of Aboriginal people from across the NT.”

Turner said it was “clearer than ever” that the federal government needed to strengthen its powers to intervene on projects that affected water and aquatic ecosystems.

“In August, the high court quashed the NT government’s decision to grant the Singleton Station licence because they found it had been unlawfully granted,” he said.

“The way the [proposed] law is now, we wouldn’t have been able to support native title holders to challenge the merits of such a licence in the first place.

“This is especially troubling when we might be faced with future high-water-consuming developments like data centres looking to take advantage of lax regulations and free water.”

The proposed changes would scrap a legal requirement that water allocation plans set aside water for the environment to maintain rivers, springs, wetlands and water-dependent ecosystems. They are part of a larger package that would also make changes to marine pollution, heritage and mining legislation.

Other planned changes include removing a rule that total water use by industry remains below a limit set in each water allocation plan, and another that requires water resource management to comply with water allocation plans.

Environment groups said the bill would also weaken the definition of “estimated sustainable yield”, which is the amount of water that may be taken or used from a water resource.

Howey said the government risked trading the territory’s aquifers and rivers for “short-term gain and profiteering” by the gas, agriculture and tech industries.

“It’s so blatant and shameless to literally be deleting the environment’s water allocation,” she said.

“The scant safeguards that did exist – and they were threadbare – have just been ripped up altogether. They’re not even pretending any more that they’ve got an interest in protecting these places.”

The NT environment minister, Joshua Burgoyne, denied the bill dismantled environmental safeguards. He said the territory’s “core framework” of environment-related laws – including those relating to environmental assessments and approvals, mining licences, pollution control, water allocation planning and heritage protection – remained.

“Our government remains focused on facts, not the fearmongering tactics of environmental lobby groups,” he said.

The bill before the NT parliament follows a raft of earlier changes that have dismantled environment and climate protections since the CLP won government.

They include scrapping the NT’s renewable energy target, abandoning a promise to implement an emissions reduction target of 43% by 2030, and creating a territory coordinator role within the bureaucracy with the power to override 32 territory laws to fast-track developments.

Bree Ahrens, the executive director of the Environment Centre NT, said the proposal to rewrite water rules puts the needs of industry above nature. “This is a smash and grab bill that puts water and nature last,” she said.

Ahrens called on the Albanese government to rule out handing federal assessment and decision-making powers under national nature laws to “an increasingly rogue NT government that is dismantling water safeguards”.

After changes to Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act last year, the federal government can transfer its decision-making powers about whether or not a development can proceed to state and territory governments.

Watt declined to comment.

Burgoyne said the NT government had “a track record of protecting the environment, such as extending the Limmen Bight marine park”.

“We support responsible development, effective environmental and water regulation, and continuing our work to rebuild the economy and restore our unique Territory lifestyle,” he said.

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.
